bins.label: The Roman Republic
bins.note: Rule by elected magistrates for a year at a time, with the Senate and the tribunes as checks (509 to 27 BC).

bins.label: The Roman Empire
bins.note: Rule by an emperor who held the army's loyalty, after Augustus took power in 27 BC.

cards.t: Two consuls were chosen each year, and each could veto the other's decisions.
cards.why: Annual paired consuls belong to the Republic; an emperor had no equal to check him.

cards.t: Magistrates held office for one year, so no single man could keep power for long.
cards.why: Short terms were how the Republic guarded against a king.

cards.t: Tribunes of the plebs could veto laws and protect ordinary citizens from the magistrates.
cards.why: The tribunes were a Republican check; under the emperors the office lost its force.

cards.t: The Senate was the chief body of advice, and its members were mostly former magistrates.
cards.why: In the Republic the Senate steered policy; under emperors it mostly followed them.

cards.t: Augustus took the title princeps, meaning first citizen, while keeping the forms of republican government.
cards.why: Augustus founded the Empire and hid it behind Republican forms.

cards.t: Emperors commanded the armies and were guarded in Rome by the Praetorian Guard.
cards.why: Control of the soldiers was the base of an emperor's power.

cards.t: After Augustus, power passed from emperor to emperor by adoption, inheritance or seizure.
cards.why: The Republic elected its magistrates; the Empire handed on one man's power.

cards.t: Emperors came to be honoured as gods after their death.
cards.why: Worship of dead emperors began under the Empire.

cards.t: The Senate continued to meet in the city of Rome.
cards.why: The Senate sat in Rome in both periods, though its power was very different.
